en.title: Doctor Doom's Gothic Core: Avengers: Doomsday Finally Gets It Right
en.summary: The MCU's next major villain, Doctor Doom, is poised for a grand entrance in Avengers: Doomsday. Early insights suggest the film is embracing the character's true, over-the-top nature.
en.body:
For years, fans have debated how to translate the magnificent, terrifying **Doctor Doom** to the big screen. The 2005 **Fantastic Four** and its sequel leaned into a surprisingly mundane portrayal, casting **Julian McMahon** as a petulant corporate magnate. The less said about the 2015 reboot, where **Toby Kebbell** played a moody tech bro with head-exploding powers, the better. These interpretations fundamentally misunderstood a character who, since his 1962 debut in **Fantastic Four #5**, has been defined by his audacious, larger-than-life persona. Thankfully, directors **Joe and Anthony Russo** seem poised to correct this course with **Robert Downey Jr.**'s rumored take on Doom in **Avengers: Doomsday**.

Joe Russo himself has described Doom as a "Gothic character," someone "not above selling his soul to get what he wants." This statement alone signals a welcome departure from realism. Doom isn't just a villain; he's a monarch, a sorcerer, a scientist, and a tragic figure. His first comic book appearance saw him manipulating the **Fantastic Four** into traveling back to the 18th century, a plot point brimming with the kind of theatricality that has defined him for decades. Later stories, like the **Mark Waid** and **Mike Wieringo** arc "Unthinkable," cemented this, depicting Doom selling his beloved Valeria's soul to the devil for power. This is the Doom that fans have been waiting for – a villain who operates on a grand, operatic scale, unburdened by mundane reality.

## The Doom We Deserve

The prospect of **Robert Downey Jr.** embodying this version of **Doctor Doom** is electrifying. While the teaser for **Avengers: Doomsday** hints at a complex connection between Doom and Tony Stark, potentially even suggesting Doom is an alternate-universe Stark, the core of the character's appeal lies in his inherent DOOM-ness. The film is reportedly a culmination of a massive story arc involving heroes from multiple universes—Earth-616's **Avengers** and **Wakandans**, Earth-828's **Fantastic Four**, and the original **X-Men**. This multiversal clash provides the perfect backdrop for Doom's grand ambitions. His rivalry with Reed Richards is central to his character, and placing him as the primary antagonist in a film that brings together disparate realities allows for his ego and power to be showcased on an unprecedented scale.

## A Gothic Mastermind

Fans have long clamored for a cinematic **Doctor Doom** who embraces his full, often theatrical, potential. The Russos' acknowledgment of Doom's "Gothic" nature is a significant step in the right direction. It suggests an understanding that Doom's power isn't just technological or magical, but rooted in his unwavering will, his tortured psyche, and his absolute belief in his own superiority. This aligns perfectly with his comic book origins and his most compelling storylines. Previous attempts to ground him in a more conventional villain archetype have fallen flat precisely because they stripped away the very essence of what makes **Doctor Doom** such an enduring and fascinating character. The promise of a Doom who is "not above selling his soul" is a powerful indicator that **Avengers: Doomsday** might finally deliver the villain fans have dreamed of.

## What's Next

**Avengers: Doomsday** is set to release in 47 days, promising a multiversal spectacle. With **Doctor Doom** at its center, the film has the potential to redefine MCU villainy, finally giving the iconic character the grand, gothic stage he deserves.

content_raw: How do you solve a problem like Victor Von Doom? Don’t ask the producers of the previous two live-action outings of Doctor Doom . The 2005 Fantastic Four movie and its 2007 sequel asked the late Julian McMahon to stay in Nip/Tuck mode, playing Doom as a petulant rich kid running a Fortune 500 company. The 2015 film was even worse, casting Toby Kebbell as Doom a pouty computer nerd who later developed the power to make people’s heads explode. This is a guy who speaks in the third person and wears a green tunic over his metallic armor, a master of the scientific and mystic arts. So why is everyone trying to make him realistic? Thankfully, Joe and Anthony Russo don’t seem to be taking that direction for Robert Downey Jr. ‘s version of Doom in Avengers: Doomsday . “Doom is a Gothic character,” Joe Russo told Empire Magazine , describing him as someone who’s “not above selling his soul to get what he wants.” But as much as it sounds like the Russos are finally doing right by Doom, they then go onto self report a fundamental mistake about the character. First, let’s talk about what they get right: Doctor Doom is absolutely a Gothic character. Since his first appearance in 1962’s Fantastic Four #5, by Jack Kirby and Stan Lee , Doom has gone over-the-top. In that first story, Doom’s plot involved sending the FF back to the 18th century, where the Thing becomes the new Blackbeard the Pirate. Modern incarnations of the character have fleshed him out, but never backed away from his over-the-top audacity. In the 2003 Fantastic Four arc, Unthinkable , by Mark Waid and Mike Wieringo, Doom sells the soul of his beloved Valeria to the devil, so he can gain the power to destroy the FF for good. In 2015’s Secret Wars , by Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribić, Doom makes himself into the God Emperor of a Marvel Universe that he rebuilt in his image. He conquered the planet in last year’s One World Under Doom , by Ryan North and R. B. Silva, and he became the King of Hell in the recent Captain America comics by Chip Zdarsky and Valerio Schiti. Simply put, Doom is imperious and ambitious, to a degree that would be absurd if he didn’t take it all so deadly seriously, resulting in a character who is thrillingly operatic. According to most versions of his origin, Doom was the son of Romani peasants living in Latveria. Made arrogant by his scientific genius, Doom went to America, where he studied alongside Reed Richards. So bold was Doom that he refused to listen when Reed pointed out an error in the calculations used for a device he built, and when the machine exploded, he blamed Reed and not himself for the failure. That explosion did something to Doom’s face. It may have completely disfigured him, or it may have left a small scar.
